strengths: Comprehensive, multi-backbone study: the paper trains the same 8M-sample spatial corpus on three architecturally distinct foundation families (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel, spanning 2B–8B), which strengthens the claim that data scaling—rather than a specific architecture—drives the gains, and yields consistent improvements (e.g., InternVL3-8B: 68.7 on VSI, 43.3 on MMSI, 85.6 on MindCube).

The taxonomy-driven data construction (five capabilities with a layered Perspective-taking hierarchy: view correspondence, camera motion, allocentric transformation) is well motivated and addresses genuinely underrepresented task types (PT, MR) that prior corpora (SpatialVLM, VSI-590K, SpatialLadder) under-serve.

The shortcut/overfitting analysis (Sec. 5.5) is a notable strength: no-vision evaluation on MindCube, VSI-Debiased comparison against Cambrian-S, and circular tests show SenseNova-SI degrades far less (85.6→52.5 no-vision; only 10 points under Hard circular) than prior SoTA (which is essentially language-prior-driven), supporting the claim of genuine visual grounding.

Additional analyses add value beyond the leaderboard result: frame-count extrapolation (Tab. 2, trained on ≤16 frames yet improving at 32–64), controlled single-dataset spill-over experiments (Fig. 3), a sober negative/neutral result on text-based spatial CoT (Tab. 4), and a no-finetuning downstream robotics validation on EmbodiedBench (Tab. 5).

Honest scoping in places: the paper concedes saturation trends, acknowledges CoT results are preliminary, and notes MindCube results converge to ~50 without vision, implicitly endorsing benchmark debiasing.

Comparison protocol appears careful: most baseline numbers are re-verified on the EASI harness with official prompts rather than copied, with citations marked (†) where results come from original papers.
weaknesses: Training–evaluation circularity is insufficiently resolved. The corpus 'incorporates all' of several community datasets (Sec. 3.2), including VSI-590K, MindCube, ViCA, VLM-3R, MultiSpa—while the headline results are reported on VSI-Bench and MindCube(-Tiny). The paper only asserts 'non-overlapping' splits for MindCube without describing the decontamination procedure (scene-level vs. QA-level overlap, seed scenarios shared with VSI-Bench scans). Given [4]'s own 'train on the test set' warning cited in the paper, a rigorous contamination audit is needed before 'state-of-the-art' claims are credible.

Limited technical novelty beyond scale. The approach is continued SFT on curated data with no architectural or algorithmic contribution; the claimed 'scaling law of spatial intelligence' is not formalized—no fitted curves, no controlled data-scaling ablations isolating each capability or dataset source, and the 'emergence' claims rest on qualitative case examples (Fig. 3) with small sample sizes (e.g., 90.4%, 66.7% on single sub-categories) rather than systematic transfer experiments with baselines and confidence intervals.

Missing reproducibility detail for the 4.5M synthesized samples: the QA-generation pipeline over ScanNet/ScanNet++/Matterport3D/CA-1M/Ego-Exo4D is described only at a high level—no templates, filtering, label noise rates, human verification, or quality-control statistics are provided. For a data-centric paper, this is a material omission, and the Model/Code fields on page 1 are empty.

Internal inconsistencies undermine polish: the abstract reports '50.1% on SITE' while the flagship InternVL3-8B achieves 47.7 (50.1 belongs to the Qwen3-VL-8B variant); the corpus is called 'SenseNova-SI-8M' but Sec. 3.2 totals 8.5M; Sec. 5.3.2/5.5 cite 'MindCube-SFT-RawQA [54]' in Tab. 3 while the text attributes it to [57]. The framing ('an ongoing project, and this report will be updated continuously') reads as a tech report rather than a self-contained conference contribution.

Key supporting claims lack evidence or scope: 'capability synergy' (limited CR data transferring to Comprehensive Reasoning) is asserted from one curve; the 2B-vs-8B PT divergence is only hypothesized, with no probing or analysis; 'outperforms GPT-5 in specific spatial abilities' relies on sub-capability averages whose composition (benchmark subsets per capability) is defined only via Fig. 1 and not tabulated.

General-capability retention is evaluated on a single benchmark (MMBench-En); small drops are noted for Qwen3-VL-8B (−1.30) and InternVL3-2B (−1.00), but broader regression testing (e.g., Video-MME, grounding, OCR-heavy tasks) would be needed to support 'retention' claims, especially with 8M task-specific samples in the mix.

The CoT study, while interesting, confounds several variables (answer-conditioned GPT-5 rationales, differing token budgets 1→2263 tokens) and is evaluated on a single VSI subset, so the sweeping conclusion that text CoT 'may signal the need for a paradigm shift' is not well supported by one preliminary experiment.

strengths: The core contribution—a systematically organized 8.5M-sample spatial training corpus spanning five capability categories (MM, SR, PT, MR, CR) with particular attention to previously underexplored perspective-taking tasks—is a tangible, useful resource for the community.

Results are validated across three heterogeneous backbone families (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel), showing consistent large gains (e.g., +63.2% on VSI-Bench for InternVL3-8B), which strengthens the claim that the improvement is data-driven rather than architecture-specific.

The robustness analysis is more careful than typical: evaluation on VSI-Debiased, no-vision testing on MindCube (85.6 → 52.5, contrasting with MindCube-RawQA-SFT's 50.7 with no images), and circular choice-reordering tests provide meaningful evidence against language-shortcut explanations.
Frame-count extrapolation experiments (Tab. 2) are an interesting ablation showing generalization beyond the 16-frame training regime, outperforming Cambrian-S-7B with far fewer inference frames.

The negative result on spatial chain-of-thought (Tab. 4)—that text CoT variants yield limited gains over simple QA scaling—is a useful, honestly reported observation with potential to redirect future work.
Downstream validation on EmbodiedBench without finetuning (16.6→33.3 success rate on the spatial subset) provides some evidence of practical utility beyond benchmark scores.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination is not adequately addressed. Roughly 3.3M of the training samples come from community datasets (VSI-590K, MindCube, ViCA, VLM-3R, etc.), and evaluation is on benchmarks derived from overlapping source material: VSI-590K is built from ScanNet-style indoor video (the same source as VSI-Bench), and SITE unifies 'over thirty datasets' that may intersect the training corpora. MindCube-10K vs. MindCube-Tiny are claimed non-overlapping, but no decontamination analysis (e.g., scene/video-level overlap checks) is reported for VSI-Bench or SITE, so the headline SOTA numbers may partly reflect training on distributionally identical data.

The paper is written and formatted as an ongoing tech report rather than a rigorous scientific contribution: the 'Model:' and 'Code:' fields on page 1 are empty, so the central reproducibility claim ('all models publicly released') is unverifiable at submission time, and essential details (data generation QA procedures, mixing ratios, filtering, deduplication) are absent.

The 'scaling law' claim is under-supported. Fig. 1 shows qualitative curves, but the construction of the scaling points (which data subsets at each stage), the confidence-band computation, and fit to any quantitative scaling relationship are never specified. No controlled ablations isolate the contribution of the 4.5M newly generated samples versus the 3.3M aggregated community samples versus the 0.6M general QA data, even though 'data mixing is highly effective' is presented as a key finding.

Claims of 'emergent generalization' rest on a handful of hand-picked examples (Fig. 3) with specific per-case accuracies (90.4%, 23.8%, etc.) and no systematic transfer evaluation, sample sizes, or baseline comparisons; 'emergence' is a strong term for what is shown.

The 'outperforms GPT-5' framing is selective: GPT-5 exceeds SenseNova-SI on MMSI (41.8 vs. 43.3 is close), SITE (61.8 vs. 47.7/50.1), and MM items; superiority holds mainly on PT and MindCube, the latter being the benchmark most exposed to same-distribution training data.

Evaluation of general-capability retention relies on a single benchmark (MMBench-En); broader general benchmarks (e.g., MM-Vet, MathVista, OCR tasks) and generative quality would be needed to substantiate the no-forgetting claim, particularly for the unified model Bagel.

The CoT study, while interesting, is limited to one task subset (VSI Object Relative Direction) and 100K examples, limiting the generality of the conclusion that text-based CoT is not the right paradigm for spatial reasoning.

Presentation quality is below conference standard: repeated typos ('Foudational', 'udnerstanding', 'capbilities', 'SoTA'), and several result inconsistencies between the abstract (SITE 50.1%) and the best-model table entry (47.7%) that are never reconciled.

The one-epoch, single-hyperparameter training scheme (LR 5e-6, batch 2048) is presented without any sensitivity analysis or justification, making it hard to judge whether reported gains are optimized or incidental.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic data curation: SenseNova-SI-8M aggregates 4M open-source samples and generates 4.5M new QA pairs organized under a principled capability taxonomy (MM, SR, MR, PT, CR), explicitly targeting underrepresented capabilities such as perspective-taking (PT), which prior datasets largely overlooked.

Broad empirical validation: results span three architecturally distinct base models (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel), showing consistent gains across five spatial benchmarks (e.g., 68.7 VSI-Bench, 43.3 MMSI, 85.6 MindCube-Tiny) while preserving general multimodal performance on MMBench-En — this cross-family consistency strengthens the claim that gains stem from data scaling rather than architecture-specific effects.

Unusually rigorous robustness analysis for this type of paper: evaluation on VSI-Debiased, no-vision testing on MindCube, and Soft/Hard circular tests convincingly demonstrate that SenseNova-SI is less reliant on language shortcuts and answer-ordering biases than the prior SoTA (MindCube-RawQA-SFT drops from 85.6 to 52.5 without vision, vs. near-identical blind performance for the baseline). This directly addresses the most common criticism of benchmark-targeted SFT.

Honest and informative negative results: the spatial CoT study (Tab. 4) shows that even carefully engineered CogMap-style CoT yields marginal gains over QA-style scaling, a useful counterpoint to prevailing trends; the frame-extrapolation ablation (Tab. 2) provides evidence of genuine spatial structure learning beyond the 16-frame training window.

Downstream validation on EmbodiedBench without finetuning (16.6 vs 10.4 OP) ties the benchmark gains to practical embodied utility, and the stated commitment to open-source release increases community value.
The frame-extrapolation result (comparable to Cambrian-S-7B using half or quarter of the inference frames) is a compelling, well-isolated finding.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence: the abstract and title say 'eight million samples' / 'SI-8M', but Sec. 3.2 and Fig. 2 state a total corpus of 8.5M QA pairs; the abstract's headline numbers (68.7 VSI, 43.3 MMSI, 85.6 MindCube, 54.6 ViewSpatial, 47.7... yet SITE listed as 50.1) mix results from different model variants (InternVL3-8B vs. Qwen3-VL-8B), presenting a composite best-of-family rather than a single model's profile — this should be stated explicitly.

No controlled ablation of the data mixture. The central claim that extensive PT data drives the gains (Sec. 5.2.1, 5.3.1) is asserted but never isolated experimentally (e.g., training with/without the newly generated PT corpus, or with MM/SR-only mixtures). Given that this is the paper's main scientific hypothesis, the missing ablation is a material gap.

Potential train–test contamination is insufficiently discussed. The training corpus incorporates community datasets (VSI-590K, MindCube data, SAT, CLEVR, etc.), and SITE aggregates over thirty datasets that plausibly overlap with training sources. The MindCube evaluation follows the official non-overlapping split, but for VSI-Bench, ViewSpatial, and SITE the degree of source-level overlap with training data is not quantified — this weakens the 'emergent generalization' narrative.

The 'emergence' and 'spill-over' claims (Sec. 5.4.1, Fig. 3) rest on a small number of case studies with single-task transfer percentages; no controlled large-scale quantification (e.g., aggregate transfer across held-out task families with baseline comparisons) is provided, so 'emergent generalization' is overstated relative to the evidence.

The 'scaling law' framing is loose: no functional fits, exponents, or statistical treatment of the saturation trends are given; conclusions rest on visual inspection of Fig. 1 curves whose data-point counts and per-benchmark subtask averaging are not fully specified.

Training/evaluation protocol details are thin for reproducibility: single hyperparameter setting (one epoch, fixed LR) with no sensitivity analysis, no seeds/variance for the tabulated results, and the Model/Code links in the abstract are empty at submission time despite the release claim.

Presentation issues: typos ('Multimodal Foudational Models', 'spatial udnerstanding'), and the caption/abstract inconsistency about SITE (50.1 vs. 47.7) suggest the manuscript was assembled hastily in places.

strengths: Substantial and systematic data contribution: the paper curates and balances an 8.5M-sample spatial intelligence corpus organized under a principled five-capability taxonomy (MM, SR, MR, PT, CR), explicitly targeting the underrepresented perspective-taking (PT) capability that prior datasets largely ignored. The data construction pipeline (unified annotation, object/image selection, ambiguity reduction, balanced sampling, Appendix B) is described in unusually concrete detail.

Strong empirical results validated across three heterogeneous backbones (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel), showing consistent gains and SOTA performance on five recent spatial benchmarks (e.g., 68.7 VSI-Bench, 85.6 MindCube) with 2B/7B/8B models, exceeding both proprietary models (GPT-5 on PT) and dedicated spatial models (VST, Cambrian-S) at comparable data scale.

Careful anti-shortcut evaluation: the paper goes beyond leaderboard numbers with VSI-Debiased testing, no-vision ablations on MindCube (revealing that the prior SOTA relies almost entirely on language priors), and circular test designs — this materially strengthens the credibility of the claimed gains.

Informative analyses: single-dataset training experiments (Tab. 6) provide a useful community resource on dataset complementarity; scaling curves (Tab. 7) show monotone gains up to 8M samples; the frame extrapolation ablation (Tab. 2) is a genuinely interesting finding (trained at ≤16 frames, generalizes to 64+); the negative result that three text-based CoT schemes yield limited gains for spatial reasoning is a valuable, honestly reported preliminary study.

Downstream validation on EmbodiedBench manipulation tasks without finetuning (+59.6% over the base model) demonstrates practical utility beyond benchmark scores, and the models are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility and community impact.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core approach is data curation plus supervised fine-tuning on existing foundation models without architectural or training-algorithm changes. For a CVPR paper, the contribution rests almost entirely on data scale/quality and evaluation, and the 'scaling law' framing (Sec. 5.3) is loose — the experiments are incremental data-mixture scaling on one primary backbone rather than controlled scaling-law analysis across model sizes, so the saturation/model-size claims (e.g., the 2B PT hypothesis) remain speculative.

Potential train/test overlap is only partially addressed. The training corpus includes VSI-590K, MindCube training data, and other community datasets while evaluation targets VSI-Bench, MindCube, and ViewSpatial; the paper claims non-overlapping splits and provides debiased/no-vision/circular analyses, but a direct contamination audit (e.g., scene-level or image-level overlap statistics between SenseNova-SI-8M and the evaluation sets) is not reported. The no-vision result on MindCube (50.7 vs. 52.5 blind baseline) leaves open how much of the visual gain is grounded versus text-prior synergy.

Several headline claims are supported by thin evidence: 'emergent generalization' and 'meta-tasks' rest on a handful of qualitative case studies (Fig. 3) without quantitative transfer measurements or error bars; the capability-synergy claim (PT/SR gains transferring to CR) is asserted from aggregate curves rather than controlled experiments.

The 4.5M 'further scaling' data is generated from only six 3D sources (MessyTable, ScanNet, ScanNet++, SUN RGB-D, CA-1M, Ego-Exo4D, Matterport3D), which risks distributional narrowness (indoor, scan-derived scenes) that is not analyzed; the paper acknowledges ' saturation' but does not isolate whether gains come from PT data specifically versus sheer volume — an ablation removing PT data is missing.

Presentation and rigor gaps: no variance/significance reporting for the main table (Fig. 1 shows ±0.5 std but Tab. 1 does not), the training details are sparse (single epoch, one LR, no data-mixture ratios per capability), and the report is explicitly framed as an 'ongoing project' technical report, which weakens its fit as a finished research contribution.

Some comparisons are asymmetric: results for VST and Cambrian-S are partly cited directly from their papers while SenseNova-SI results are re-run under the EASI protocol, and inference-time differences (frame counts, prompting variants OP/SIP) complicate direct comparability.

strengths: Comprehensive data curation: the paper builds a large 8.5M-sample corpus organized under a principled taxonomy (EASI-based capabilities), addresses an underexplored capability (perspective-taking), and provides useful dataset-level ablations (Table 6) that show no single dataset covers spatial intelligence comprehensively - a genuinely informative resource for the community.

Multi-backbone validation: the same data recipe is applied to InternVL3 (2B/8B), Qwen3-VL, and the unified Bagel model, showing consistent gains (+15% to +53% relative on spatial benchmarks). This strengthens the claim that the improvement is data-driven rather than architecture-specific.

Careful anti-shortcut evaluation: the paper goes beyond raw benchmark scores by evaluating on VSI-Debiased, running no-vision controls (Table 3 shows prior SOTA MindCube-RawQA-SFT scores ~50.7 without images, while SenseNova-SI drops to 52.5), and circular tests. This is a methodologically responsible evaluation practice.

The CoT study (Sec 5.6) is honest and somewhat informative: all three text-CoT variants yield marginal gains despite large token overhead, with the negative result discussed candidly and case studies provided in the appendix.
Frame-count extrapolation analysis (Table 2) and scaling curves (Table 7, Fig. 1) provide some empirical insight into how spatial capability scales with data and inference frames.
weaknesses: Limited scientific novelty: the core contribution is a data-engineering effort (aggregating public datasets plus template-generated QA from 3D scans). There is no new architecture, training objective, or algorithmic insight. Several concurrent works (VST, Cambrian-S, SpatialLadder) follow essentially the same recipe; the delta is scale and the emphasis on perspective-taking data.

Potential benchmark contamination undermines headline claims: training data includes VSI-590K, MindCube-10K, and ViewSpatial-related sources, and evaluation uses VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial-Bench built from the same underlying scenes/datasets (the footnote 'MindCube* denotes MindCube directly quantized' suggests close coupling). Comparisons against GPT-5 and other models that never saw these training distributions are therefore not apples-to-apples, and the paper does not report contamination checks or decontamination procedures for the 4.5M self-generated samples.

The 'emergent generalization' claims rest on anecdotal evidence: Fig. 3 shows a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples (four cases) with no quantitative cross-task transfer measurements, no baselines, and no statistical support. Labeling these 'early signs of emergent spatial intelligence' overstates the evidence considerably.

The 'scaling law of spatial intelligence' framing is loose: Table 7 shows gains that saturate after ~3-4M samples, which the authors themselves concede is saturation, not a law. No curve fitting, no controlled capacity/data regimes beyond two model sizes, and the 2B-vs-8B PT divergence (Sec 5.3.1) is only 'hypothesized' without further experiments.

Some benchmark results are weak or negative and underexplored: SITE drops to 47.7 for the 8B model (below Qwen3-VL-8B's 45.8 only marginally, and below the best proprietary models), MMBench-EN slightly degrades for two variants, and Table 8 shows declines on MMStar/AI2D/OCR for most variants - contradicting to some degree the general-capability retention claim in Sec 5.2.2.

Reproducibility gaps: the Codebase and Models links in the abstract are empty placeholders; the 4.5M generated QA pipeline is described only at a high level (appendix B gives filtering heuristics but no prompts for the VLM-annotated descriptions, no data release confirmation for the generated portion, no exact QA templates).

Presentation issues: the claimed 'surpasses GPT-5' narrative holds only on selected subsets (e.g., PT), while GPT-5 or Gemini-3 leads on MMSI, MindCube, ViewSpatial, and SITE overall (Tables 9-13); the abstract phrasing is more optimistic than the tables. Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse; terminology like 'Meta-task' and 'capability synergy' is used loosely without definition.

The downstream EmbodiedBench experiment (Table 5) compares against only GPT-4o and the base InternVL3-8B with a single prompt variant, without fine-tuning baselines or other spatial models, making its practical significance hard to judge.

strengths: Comprehensive and large-scale data effort: SenseNova-SI-8M is systematically organized under a principled capability taxonomy (MM, SR, MR, PT, CR), explicitly targeting underrepresented capabilities like perspective-taking, with a detailed appendix documenting annotation, filtering, frame selection (Algorithm 1), and QA quality control (Appendix B).

Strong and broad empirical results: consistent improvements across three distinct base model families (InternVL3, Qwen3-VL, Bagel), achieving best open-source results on five spatial benchmarks (e.g., 68.7 VSI-Bench, 85.6 MindCube) while retaining general multimodal performance (Tab. 1, Tab. 8).

Rigorous robustness analysis: the paper does not just report headline gains; it uses VSI-Debiased, no-vision testing, and circular tests (Tab. 2, Tab. 3) to show the model is less reliant on language shortcuts than prior baselines — a notable and careful validation that many similar data-scaling works omit.

Useful scaling analysis: single-dataset training results (Tab. 6), data-scaling curves (Tab. 7, Fig. 1), and frame-count extrapolation experiments (Tab. 2) provide genuinely informative findings for the community, e.g., 2B models diverging on PT tasks and capability synergy transferring to CR tasks.
The preliminary CoT study (Sec. 5.6, Tab. 4, Appendix H) is a negative-but-valuable result, honestly reporting that text-based CoT yields limited gains, with plausible hypotheses and case studies.
Models are stated to be publicly released, and downstream validation on EmbodiedBench (Tab. 5) demonstrates practical utility beyond benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is systematic data curation and continued SFT on existing base models; there is no architectural, algorithmic, or training-paradigm innovation, which places the paper closer to a technical report than a novel research contribution.

Potential train/test overlap is not fully addressed: training data includes sources (e.g., VSI-590K/ScanNet, MindCube-10K) closely related to evaluation benchmarks (VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny), and several synthetic data sources (ScanNet, MessyTable, Matterport3D) underlie the evaluated benchmarks. The shortcut analyses (Sec. 5.5) partially mitigate this concern, but a scene-level deduplication analysis between training scenes and benchmark scenes is missing.

Some claims are over-stated: the abstract claims SOTA on five benchmarks, yet on SITE (47.7–50.1 vs GPT-5 61.8, Gemini-3 62.2) and MMSI (43.3 vs Gemini-3 45.2) proprietary models still lead; 'emergent generalization' (Sec. 5.4) is supported mainly by a handful of qualitative case studies (Fig. 3) rather than systematic quantitative evidence.

The scaling analysis is conducted in depth only for InternVL3-8B (Tab. 7); scaling behavior across the other two model families is not reported, weakening the generality of the 'scaling law of spatial intelligence' claim.

Some inconsistencies and presentation issues: abstract reports SITE 50.1 while the flagship model reports 47.7 (the 50.1 belongs to the Qwen3-VL variant); empty Codebase/Models links in the abstract; typos ('Multimodal Foudational Models', 'capbilities'); Fig. 1 is dense and hard to read; statistical significance/standard deviations over runs are not reported for main tables.

Reproducibility is only partially supported at review time: training details are relatively brief (one paragraph, Sec. 4), the data generation pipeline for 4.5M newly curated samples is described at a high level, and the promised release links are not yet available.
